concept.name: Bitmask Dynamic Programming

relationships.description: Connects Bitmask Dynamic Programming to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Bitmask DP encodes a subset of $n \le 20$ elements as an integer $0 \dots 2^n - 1$, turning exponential factorial permutations ($n!$) into polynomial-in-subset DP ($O(n^2 2^n)$ or $O(n 2^n)$).
spark.keyTakeaway: Whenever a problem tracks which items from a small set ($n \le 20$) have been visited or assigned, pack the subset into an integer bitmask and transition by setting one bit at a time.

concept.whyItMatters: Brute-force permutation search over $n = 20$ items evaluates $20! \approx 2.4 \times 10^{18}$ states—impossible even on a cluster. Bitmask DP collapses all permutations that share the same visited set and last element into a single state, shrinking $2.4 \times 10^{18}$ down to $20 \times 2^{20} \approx 2.1 \times 10^7$ states, which solves in under 100 ms in C++/Java.
whenToUse: Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and shortest Hamiltonian path/cycle over $n \le 20$ nodes (Held-Karp algorithm).
Exact bipartite matching, task assignment, or partitioning into $k$ equal-sum subsets when $n \le 20$.
Sum over Subsets (SOS) DP and broken-profile / grid-tiling DP where each column state is a bitmask of height $H \le 12$.
whenNotToUse: Inputs with $n > 22$—$2^{25} \approx 3.3 \times 10^7$ states already exceeds typical memory/time budgets unless using meet-in-the-middle.
Problems where order does not matter beyond item counts (use standard knapsack or frequency DP instead).
Large-scale routing ($n > 50$) where heuristics, ILP/MIP solvers, or Christofides approximation are required.
keyPoints: State compression: bit $i$ of `mask` is `1` iff element $i$ is included, mapping any subset $S \subseteq \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ to an array index `[0 .. (1 << n) - 1]`.
Held-Karp TSP recurrence: `dp[mask | (1 << nxt)][nxt] = min(dp[mask | (1 << nxt)][nxt], dp[mask][cur] + dist[cur][nxt])`.
Canonical assignment optimization: when assigning item $i$ to worker $k$, you only need `dp[mask]` (not `dp[i][mask]`) because `popcount(mask)` uniquely determines $i$!
Iterative topological order: `mask` strictly increases whenever you set a new bit (`mask | (1 << j)` > `mask`), so a flat `for mask in range(1 << n)` loop is always a valid DP order.
Submask-transition complexity: iterating `sub = (sub - 1) & rem` across all `mask` values takes $\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} 2^{n-k} = 3^n$ total operations—feasible up to $n \le 15$.

examples.title: Last-Mile Delivery Route Optimization (Held-Karp TSP)
examples.scenario: A courier dispatcher computes the exact minimum-time route across 16 drop-off stops from a depot using asymmetric traffic travel times.
examples.outcome: Held-Karp bitmask DP (`dp[1 << 16][16]`, ~1M states) computes the exact optimal tour in ~15 ms in Java/C++, beating greedy nearest-neighbor by 12–18%.

examples.title: Worker-to-Job Minimum Cost Assignment
examples.scenario: Assigning 18 specialized jobs to 18 workers with an $18 \times 18$ cost matrix where certain pairs are incompatible.
examples.outcome: Using `k = Integer.bitCount(mask)` as the current worker index reduces state from $18 \cdot 2^{18}$ to just $2^{18}$ (262,144 ints = 1 MB), solving in <10 ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Bottom-up loops over `mask = 0 .. (1<<n)-1` avoid recursion overhead and are cache-friendly.
tradeOffs.con: Top-down DFS with memoization skips unreachable masks (e.g., when graph edges are sparse or constraints prune branches).

tradeOffs.factor: Dropped Dimension via `popcount(mask)` vs. Explicit Index
tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates an entire $O(n)$ memory dimension (e.g., shrinking 20 MB to 1 MB) when elements are processed in fixed order.
tradeOffs.con: Only applies when the number of set bits uniquely identifies the current step (assignment), not when order among chosen items matters (TSP).

tradeOffs.pro: Submask iteration handles arbitrary non-associative subset merges directly.
tradeOffs.con: At $n = 18$, $3^{18} \approx 3.87 \times 10^8$ ops times out, whereas SOS DP ($18 \cdot 2^{18} \approx 4.7 \times 10^6$) finishes in milliseconds.

failureModes.name: Memory Explosion on 2D State Table
failureModes.description: Allocating `dp[1 << 20][20]` as 64-bit integers consumes $20 \times 2^{20} \times 8 = 160$ MB, triggering OOM in tight 64–128 MB sandboxes.
failureModes.mitigation: Use 32-bit `int` when values fit, drop redundant dimensions via `popcount(mask)`, or store `dp[last][mask]` for better cache locality.

failureModes.name: Wrong `3^n` vs `4^n` Bound Estimation
failureModes.description: Looping over all `mask` and all `sub` independently costs $O(4^n)$, timing out at $n = 14$ ($2.6 \times 10^8$), whereas enumerating submasks of the complement costs $O(3^n)$.
failureModes.mitigation: Always iterate `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` (or `& (~mask & FULL)`) instead of checking `if (sub & mask) == sub` over $2^n$.

failureModes.name: Python Per-State Overhead Timeout
failureModes.description: Even when $n \cdot 2^n \approx 10^7$ is small enough for C++/Java, pure Python nested loops over $10^7$ states take >5 seconds.
failureModes.mitigation: Precompute bit-transitions outside inner loops, prune unreachable masks, or use `lru_cache` / iterative arrays in C++/Java for $n \ge 17$.

failureModes.name: Missing Base Case / Unreachable Mask Guard
failureModes.description: Transitioning from `dp[mask]` initialized to `INF` without checking `if dp[mask] == INF: continue` wastes time and risks arithmetic overflow.
failureModes.mitigation: Skip unreachable states early and check `mask & (1 << i)` before transitioning.

commonMistakes: Writing `1 << n` in Python/Java without checking if $n$ actually fits within the $2^n$ time/memory budget ($n \le 20$ for $O(n 2^n)$, $n \le 15$ for $O(3^n)$).
Storing `dp[mask][last]` when `dp[mask]` alone suffices (such as worker-job assignment where `worker = popcount(mask)`).
Forgetting to check `if (mask & (1 << nxt)) != 0: continue` when extending a path, allowing vertices to be revisited.
Using `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` without handling `sub == 0` if the empty submask is a valid base or transition.
Checking `if (sub & mask) == sub` inside a $0 \dots 2^n-1$ inner loop, accidentally turning $O(3^n)$ into $O(4^n)$.

sections.content:
## The idea

When a problem's state depends on *which* subset of $n$ items has been used, any permutation of those items that ends at the same item (or has no order dependency) is equivalent. Bitmask DP represents that subset as an $n$-bit integer `mask` where bit $i$ is `1` if item $i$ is in the subset. Setting a single bit (`mask | (1 << j)`) strictly increases the integer value, which guarantees a natural DAG over `[0 .. 2^n - 1]` and collapses $O(n!)$ search into $O(n 2^n)$ or $O(n^2 2^n)$.

## Concrete walkthrough

Solve shortest Hamiltonian path (visiting all 4 nodes `0, 1, 2, 3` starting at `0`):

1. **Init**: `dp[1 << 0][0] = 0` (`mask = 0001`), all other `dp[mask][u] = INF`.
2. **Mask `0001` (`{0}`)**: From `u = 0`, try unvisited `v in {1, 2, 3}`. Set `dp[0011][1] = dist[0][1]`, `dp[0101][2] = dist[0][2]`, `dp[1001][3] = dist[0][3]`.
3. **Mask `0011` (`{0, 1}`)**: From `u = 1`, transition to unvisited `v = 2` -> `dp[0111][2] = min(..., dp[0011][1] + dist[1][2])` and `v = 3` -> `dp[1011][3]`.
4. **Final**: After all masks up to `1111` (`(1 << 4) - 1`) finish, the answer is `min(dp[1111][u] for u in range(4))`.

sections.content:
## Feasibility bounds by n

Before committing to bitmask DP, check $n$ against the transition complexity:

- **$n \le 20$ with $O(n 2^n)$** (e.g., assignment): $20 \times 10^6 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ ops — fast in C++/Java.
- **$n \le 18$ with $O(n^2 2^n)$** (e.g., TSP): $324 \times 262,144 \approx 8.5 \times 10^7$ ops — near the 1-second limit.
- **$n \le 15$ with $O(3^n)$** (submask DP): $3^{15} \approx 1.4 \times 10^7$ ops — safe; $n = 17$ ($1.3 \times 10^8$) is borderline.
- **$n \in [21, 40]$**: Switch to **Meet-in-the-Middle** ($O(2^{n/2})$) or branch-and-bound.

## Pattern comparison

| Pattern | State | Time | Space | Classic problem |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Subset Assignment | `dp[mask]` (`k = popcount(mask)`) | $O(n 2^n)$ | $O(2^n)$ | Minimum-cost worker/job matching |
| Held-Karp TSP | `dp[mask][last]` | $O(n^2 2^n)$ | $O(n 2^n)$ | Shortest Hamiltonian tour |
| Submask Partition | `dp[mask]` over `sub = (sub-1)&mask` | $O(3^n)$ | $O(2^n)$ | Partition into $k$ groups / Steiner tree |
| SOS DP | `dp[mask]` over $i = 0..n-1$ | $O(n 2^n)$ | $O(2^n)$ | Sum over all subsets of `mask` |

## Failure modes

- **OOM from 2D `long` table**: `long[1 << 20][20]` uses 160 MB; swap dimensions or pack values into `int` when possible.
- **Accidental $O(4^n)$ submask loop**: Iterating `0..2^n-1` inside `0..2^n-1` instead of `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` turns $1.4 \times 10^7$ into $1.07 \times 10^9$ ops at $n = 15$.
- **Ignoring disconnected graphs**: Returning `dp[FULL][u]` without checking `< INF` when no Hamiltonian path exists.

## Sum over Subsets (SOS) DP

When you need `F[mask] = sum(A[sub] for sub subset of mask)` for all $2^n$ masks, naive submask iteration takes $O(3^n)$. SOS DP reduces this to $O(n 2^n)$ by adding one bit dimension at a time:

`for i in range(n): for mask in range(1 << n): if mask & (1 << i): F[mask] += F[mask ^ (1 << i)]`

This exact loop computes subset sums over $2^{20}$ masks in ~20 million additions.

## Practical checklist

- Verify $n$ fits the complexity budget ($n \le 20$ for $O(n 2^n)$, $n \le 15$ for $O(3^n)$).
- Check whether `popcount(mask)` eliminates an explicit index dimension.
- Guard unreachable states (`if dp[mask] == INF: continue`) before inner transitions.
- Use `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` for $O(3^n)$ submask enumeration, never brute-force $O(4^n)$.
- Precompute `FULL_MASK = (1 << n) - 1` and use `1L << i` in Java / `1ULL << i` in C++.

interviewProblems.title: Bitmask Dynamic Programming
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Bitmask Dynamic Programming. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Bitmask DP encodes a subset of $n \le 20$ elements as an integer $0 \dots 2^n - 1$, turning exponential factorial permutations ($n!$) into polynomial-in-subset DP ($O(n^2 2^n)$ or $O(n 2^n)$).

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: DP Table dp[mask][u] applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Full Mask (1111).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Full Mask (1111) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use 32-bit `int` when values fit, drop redundant dimensions via `popcount(mask)`, or store `dp[last][mask]` for better cache locality.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Whenever a problem tracks which items from a small set ($n \le 20$) have been visited or assigned, pack the subset into an integer bitmask and transition by setting one bit at a time.
Avoid trap: Writing `1 << n` in Python/Java without checking if $n$ actually fits within the $2^n$ time/memory budget ($n \le 20$ for $O(n 2^n)$, $n \le 15$ for $O(3^n)$).
Avoid trap: Storing `dp[mask][last]` when `dp[mask]` alone suffices (such as worker-job assignment where `worker = popcount(mask)`).
When to reach for it: Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and shortest Hamiltonian path/cycle over $n \le 20$ nodes (Held-Karp algorithm).
When to reach for it: Exact bipartite matching, task assignment, or partitioning into $k$ equal-sum subsets when $n \le 20$.

putItTogether.title: Putting Bitmask Dynamic Programming Together
putItTogether.summary: Whenever a problem tracks which items from a small set ($n \le 20$) have been visited or assigned, pack the subset into an integer bitmask and transition by setting one bit at a time.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Bitmask Dynamic Programming before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Held-Karp bitmask DP (`dp[1 << 16][16]`, ~1M states) computes the exact optimal tour in ~15 ms in Java/C++, beating greedy nearest-neighbor by 12–18%.
